Need to search first.I could only read three commentaries for Jeremiah 41: Enduring Word (David Guzik), Ellicott's Commentary and the Pulpit Commentary. After that my search tool hit its usage limit and refused every further request. That means I couldn't read Gill, Matthew Henry, Precept Austin, NET Bible notes, any tradition-specific teachers, or any Catholic or Orthodox sites.

So **part 1 is covered from these three sources. Parts 2 and 3 are mostly missing.** I found no material showing Baptist, Methodist, Pentecostal, Reformed or Lutheran teachers disagreeing on this chapter. I also found nothing from Catholic, Orthodox or popular modern teaching sources, so I've left those out. The only scholarly points are the textual and critical notes that Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary report themselves, marked **[Scholarship]** below.

The three sources:
- EW = https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jeremiah-41/
- Ellicott = https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jeremiah-41.html
- Pulpit = https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jeremiah/41.htm

---

**v. 1**
- The shared meal makes the betrayal worse. Guzik cites Cundall: eating together was seen as a covenant of brotherhood, and he links it to Psalm 41:9 and John 13. Thompson suggests Gedaliah may have been making a friendly gesture. Feinberg notes that Gedaliah had been warned and still took no precautions. (EW)
- Ishmael's "royal family" line: Feinberg traces it through Elishama, a son of David (2 Samuel 5:16). (EW) The Pulpit Commentary allows either that son of David or the secretary Elishama of Jeremiah 36:12. (Pulpit)
- The visit was presented as a courtesy call to the new governor. Since the seventh month held the Feast of Tabernacles, the visitors may have claimed they were coming for the festival. Ellicott counts about three months since Jerusalem fell. (Ellicott)
- The Pulpit Commentary counts two months instead, which conflicts with Ellicott's three, and also says Gedaliah had invited them to a banquet. (Pulpit)
- **[Scholarship]** The Pulpit Commentary reports that the scholar Grätz doubted the timing. Grätz pointed to Ezekiel 33 and to the third deportation in Jeremiah 52:30, and argued that about five years, not two months, passed between the fall of the city and the murder. (Pulpit)

**v. 2**
- Guzik says Ishmael was hired by Baalis, king of Ammon (40:14), and was probably jealous of Gedaliah's appointment. (EW)
- Kidner, as Guzik cites him, says Ishmael shamed David's name: David waited for God's timing, while Ishmael acted more like Jehu. Morgan's point is that people can live through God's judgment and still ignore His word. (EW)
- Jews later kept a fast for Gedaliah's death (Zechariah 7:5; 8:19), and Thompson expects the murder to bring harsh Babylonian reprisals. (EW)
- The Pulpit Commentary dates the fast to the third day of the seventh month. That was the day the hope of a separate life in the land ended, and a new captivity followed. (Pulpit)
- Ellicott compares the scene to the Glencoe massacre: guests killing their host while he welcomed them. (Ellicott)

**v. 3**
- How could ten men do so much? Ellicott thinks the victims were mainly Gedaliah's guests, caught unarmed while feasting. The ten princes may also have brought attendants. He sees "the men of war" as narrowing who was killed. (Ellicott)
- The Pulpit Commentary says the Chaldeans were Gedaliah's bodyguard, and that both Jewish and Chaldean soldiers are meant. Non-soldiers, including the prophet, were taken captive instead (vv. 10, 16). (Pulpit)

**v. 4**
- The killings were so thorough that it took time for anyone to find out. (EW; Ellicott)
- The Pulpit Commentary says Ishmael had no personal motive for more killing. It links the further killing to Baalis's aim that the remnant should perish (40:15). (Pulpit)

**v. 5**
- These were worshippers from the old northern kingdom. Harrison suggests they descended from Judeans who moved north. Cundall and Feinberg tie them to the reforms of Hezekiah and Josiah. (EW)
- Their offerings were bloodless because animal sacrifice was no longer possible, and they came to a temple site that was still treated as holy. (EW, citing Feinberg)
- Shaving, tearing clothes and cutting themselves were signs of mourning. Both Trapp (cited in EW) and Ellicott say these practices drifted toward pagan customs the Law forbade (Leviticus 19:27; Deuteronomy 14:1). (EW; Ellicott)
- Ellicott thinks the mourning may be linked to the Day of Atonement, a fast day, or grief over the Temple. He notes they brought grain offerings and incense, not burnt offerings. (Ellicott)
- **[Scholarship]** The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) reads "Salem" for "Shiloh." Ellicott thinks this fits the order of places better; the Pulpit Commentary doubts that a city of that name existed. (Ellicott; Pulpit)
- **[Scholarship]** Because the Temple was destroyed, Thenius and Grätz guessed that Gedaliah had set up a temporary sanctuary at Mizpah. The Pulpit Commentary says 1 Maccabees 3:46 supports this. (Pulpit)

**v. 6**
- Ishmael's tears were an act to look harmless and share their grief. He invited them in using Gedaliah's name without mentioning the murder. (EW; Ellicott)
- **[Scholarship]** The Septuagint has the pilgrims weeping, not Ishmael. The Pulpit Commentary calls this reading more natural. (Ellicott; Pulpit)

**v. 7**
- Guzik's sources treat the killing as senseless cruelty. Thompson pictures a man who killed for its own sake, and Cundall notes that fouling a cistern wasted precious water. (EW)
- Ellicott offers possible motives: anger at the pilgrims' devotion, seeing their loyalty to Gedaliah as treason, revenge for his royal kin killed in 52:10, or theft. (Ellicott)

**v. 8**
- The ten men bought their lives with a bribe. (Pulpit; EW)
- The "treasures" were hidden grain pits: sealed underground stores that farmers used to protect their crops in lawless times. The Pulpit Commentary takes this from Thomson's *The Land and the Book*, and Ellicott calls the stores last year's harvest. (Pulpit; Ellicott)
- Clarke, cited by Guzik, guesses that Ishmael may have killed them anyway once he had the goods. (EW)

**v. 9**
- Asa built up Mizpah against Baasha (1 Kings 15:22; 2 Chronicles 16:6), and the pit was probably a water cistern for withstanding a siege. Ellicott also suggests it could have been a defensive trench. (EW; Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Thompson, cited by Guzik, says excavations at Tell en-Nasbeh may have found this cistern. (EW)
- **[Scholarship]** "Because of Gedaliah" can be read as "by the hand of Gedaliah," meaning Ishmael used his name as bait. Another manuscript reading is "the pit of Gedaliah." The Pulpit Commentary drops "because of" and prefers the Septuagint's "was a great pit." (Ellicott; Pulpit)

**v. 10**
- "The king's daughters" were probably princesses of the royal house. Thompson, cited by Guzik, isn't sure they were Zedekiah's own daughters. (EW; Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Ellicott says that by taking the princesses, Ishmael was claiming to represent the royal line. (Ellicott)
- Feinberg, cited by Guzik, gives three motives for taking captives: to escape punishment, to find refuge with Baalis, and to sell them as slaves. (EW)

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik says the news would have hit Johanan especially hard because he had warned Gedaliah (40:15). He praises Johanan for refusing to let the crime go unpunished. (EW)
- The "great pool" at Gibeon is the pool of 2 Samuel 2:13. Thompson, cited by Guzik, mentions the huge rock-cut pit excavated at el-Jib. (EW; Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Ellicott places Gibeon about two miles from Mizpah. He notes that Josephus puts the attack at Hebron instead, which wouldn't be on the road to Ammon. (Ellicott)
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks Ishmael may have lingered on the way so he could collect the hidden stores from v. 8. (Pulpit)

**vv. 13–14**
- Ellicott says the captives' joy shows how popular Gedaliah had been. (Ellicott)
- Kidner, cited by Guzik, says a victory that wins no hearts is empty. Guzik adds that Ishmael's violence scared even his own people. (EW)
- The Pulpit Commentary explains the old KJV phrase "cast about" as meaning "turned around." (Pulpit)

**v. 15**
- Ishmael arrived with ten men and escaped with eight, so Ellicott concludes that two died in one of the fights. (Ellicott)

**v. 16**
- Ellicott thinks the soldiers had escaped the massacre. He sees the women, children and court officials (eunuchs) as survivors of the royal household, and suggests Ebed-melech may have been among them. (Ellicott)

**v. 17**
- Geruth Chimham ("the habitation of Chimham") goes back to Chimham, son of Barzillai (2 Samuel 19:37). (EW; Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary take it to be a travellers' lodging or inn. Ellicott suggests it may even be the inn of Luke 2:7. (Ellicott; Pulpit)
- **[Scholarship]** Josephus and Aquila seem to have read it as "the hurdles of Chimham," meaning a place of sheep pens. (Pulpit)

**v. 18**
- They feared Babylon's revenge for Gedaliah's murder. (EW; Ellicott; Pulpit)
- Ellicott says the Babylonians might punish them without asking who was actually guilty. Simply having been with Ishmael could look like complicity. (Ellicott)
- The Pulpit Commentary adds that Babylon would see Ishmael as the heir of David's line, which made the fear reasonable. (Pulpit)
- Guzik says the chapter shows how chaotic and unsafe Judah was, and why Egypt looked safer. (EW)
